Press
prĕs
n., v. (a crowd; to push forward; rendering Greek ochlos and dioko)
From Latin pressare, to squeeze. In the Gospels the press is the crowd itself — the thing that has to be got through to reach Christ.

Biblical Definition

The press is a crowd, and to press is to push. Four men cannot bring their paralysed friend to Christ “for the press” and uncover the roof instead (Mar 2:4). Zacchaeus, being little of stature, “could not for the press” and climbs a sycomore (Luk 19:3). The woman with the issue of blood comes “in the press behind, and touched his garment” (Mar 5:27). Paul uses the verb of himself: “I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Php 3:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines press as to urge with force or weight; to crowd; to throng; and as a noun, a crowd, a throng, a multitude of individuals crowded together.

expand to see more

PRESS, v.t. To urge with force or weight; a word of extensive use, denoting the application of any power, physical or moral, to something that is to be moved or affected.

2. To squeeze; to crush; as, to press grapes.

PRESS, n. A crowd; a throng; a multitude of individuals crowded together.

Key Scripture

Mar 2:4 — "And when they could not come nigh unto him for the press, they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay."

Luk 19:3 — "And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature."

Mar 5:27 — "When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment."

Php 3:14 — "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Obstacles to reaching Christ are treated as providence saying no, and three Gospel stories turn on people who refused to accept the crowd as an answer.

expand to see more

Three times the press stands between someone and Christ, and three times somebody does something undignified about it. Four friends dismantle a roof over a stranger's head. A chief tax collector, a wealthy adult, climbs a tree. An unclean woman pushes through a crowd she had no legal right to be in. In each case Christ responds to what the obstacle produced — when Jesus saw their faith; make haste, and come down; thy faith hath made thee whole.

Philippians 3:14 turns the same verb inward: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. Paul had just said he had not attained. Pressing is what a man does who is not there yet and has decided that not being there yet is not a reason to stop. The word carries effort and resistance in it, which is why it is the honest verb for the Christian life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ochlos (G3793), a crowd, press; dioko (G1377), to pursue, press toward; thlibo (G2346), to press or throng.

expand to see more

Greek ochlos (G3793) — crowd, press; Mark 2:4, 5:27, Luke 19:3.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, press toward; Philippians 3:12, 14.

Greek thlibo (G2346) — to press, afflict; Mark 3:9, lest they should throng him.

Usage

"“They could not come nigh unto him for the press” — and they opened the roof."

"“Could not for the press, because he was little of stature” — so he ran and climbed."

"“I press toward the mark” — the honest verb for a man not yet arrived."
